utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody and welcome all back from recess. I hope you all had a good break and are all ready to start work and work hard. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we have the appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Novak Lukic, Boris Zorko, and our intern Ms. O'Connor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before we start, there's a little housekeeping matter to deal with. At the last appearance we were told that Exhibits P33 and P39 were admitted as public documents, and Registry informed the Trial Chamber that they contained confidential information about the identity of protected witnesses and requested that the Trial Chamber give an order on their status. The Trial Chamber indicated that it required the submissions of the parties before it can make that order, and the parties agreed that they would make such submissions after the recess. This is now after the recess. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be prepared to make some submissions after the first break, Your Honour. I was -- I'm taken aback by this. I was not informed of this, so I am not prepared. I apologise. After the recess I will make submissions on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you equally taken by surprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would actually say the same thing that Mr. Harmon said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That being the case then, we'll hear the parties after the break on -- these are Exhibits P33 and P39. Okay. Fine. Mr. Lukic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are prepared to call our next witness, Mr. Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before I hand you over to your counsel, I just want to say thank you very much for coming to testify. The Trial Chamber is advised that you may be requesting certain breaks as we go along, and should you feel the need to do so, please don't hesitate. Just ask and we'll listen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Would you be kind enough to tell your full name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I interrupt you. I'm very sorry to do this. Just for the record may the record show that the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Picard -- in the absence of Judge David. Judge Picard is right here next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, when were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 29th of April, 1950, in Kirin municipality of Vrginmost in the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in which former republic was Vrginmost?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the people's Republic of Croatia. That was what it was called when I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to go quickly through your CV because that will be important for us and the topics that we will be presenting to the Court. I'm going to put a leading question to you, and you can add if you have anything, because during our preparation for the testimony you gave some remarks regarding your CV in view of certain duties. When did you complete the military academy, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 31st of June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you about what we talked about during our preparations. After my question, would you kindly wait before you begin answering so that it can all be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I hope you can notice that the interpreter says she didn't hear the year. She heard the 31st of June but didn't hear the year, neither did we.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 31st of July, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you completed a higher school, that is, the staff command academy. When did you finish that approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I finished that academy in Belgrade in 1981 -- actually, I attended the academy from 1981 to 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you completed your post-graduate studies. Could you tell us the subject that you graduated in, and where did you attend your post-graduate studies?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed my Ph.D. in the methodology of science or the methodology of warfare. I completed that two-year study in Belgrade also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will see in your personnel file that you began your studies at the national defence school, and you suspended that education pursuant to an order by the SSNO at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This top military school for war studies was where I was sent on the 1st of September, 1991. I was there until the 23rd of September of the same year, when pursuant to an order by the SSNO I was sent to the war-affected area of the then-Yugoslavia. I went to the territory of the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this interruption in your education, did that affect only you in your class or everybody else in that class?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The education was suspended for all those who were attending the school as well as the lower school that they were attending. This is the command staff academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the schools that you completed, can you tell us what your grades were, what were your marks, generally, in those schools?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was always given the top grades in all of the schools that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to go through all of your duties, and we can see from your personnel file that in your military professional career you carried out all duties from the bottom up.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I performed all command duties from the lowest to the top one, practically the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Mr. Novakovic's personnel file on the screen now, please. This is Exhibit P1777. And this is pages 6 and 7 in the B/C/S and pages 4, 5, and 6 in the English. And we're going to go through some of the items in this personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you will see on the screen in front of you a part of your personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is ET 00611-7592 [as interpreted]. This is that page in the English. In the B/C/S this is 06 -- Ah, you have it in the B/C/S. Yes, that is right. Your Honours, I'm going to start from the entry of the 27th of April, 1990. This is the date in the right-hand column. The English page is not the right page. This refers to promotions. Can we look at the next page, please. The previous page in the English, please. We see this entry in the middle of the page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, first we can see that from 1988, pursuant to the order of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, until 1990 you were in the Koprivnica Garrison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you were assigned, pursuant to an SSNO order in April 1990, to the 5th Military District to the 73rd Motorised Brigade, and your rank at the time was colonel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the time I was lieutenant-colonel, and I was assigned to a duty that was supposed to carry the rank of colonel and that was the commander of the 73rd Motorised Brigade as it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The next entry we can see, and it's a chronological gap there, and I want to see what happened here, and that is that from August 1990, that is, the entry below the next one, pursuant to the SSNO order you were assigned as assistant chief of training of the commander of the 5th Military District in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you were sent to this training at the School for National Defence from Zagreb, where you were sent pursuant to an order of the 11th of April, 1999 [as interpreted]. As it says here in this entry, the schooling was supposed to finish on the 1st of June, 1992, but you had to leave early, and that is why the date, the 1st of July, 1992, is there -- the 1st of June, 1992, is there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: You've got the date when the order was drafted. The actual schooling was supposed to start on the 1st of September of that year, and it should have been completed in the summer of the following year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the education was suspended. And then on the 27th of September, 1992, by an order of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, you were temporarily assigned to the 5th Military District, to the 1st Operations Group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think we need to be precise here. I was not sent to the 1st Operations Group. What happened was that the command of that operations group in charge of Banija and Kordun was formed in Belgrade and I was one of the members of that command of the operative group, which, as a command that was formed in Belgrade, was sent to the area there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to discuss this further during your testimony. I'm just going through all your posts chronologically. We will deal with all of those details to the extent that they're relevant for these proceedings. After that, you were temporarily sent to the 4th Partisan Brigade in Vrginmost as part of this 1st Operations Group by a decision of the 28th of October, 1991, for a period of three months. How long were you there as the commander of the 4th Partisan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: During this time, I wasn't a commander of the 4th Partisan Brigade at all, but the commander of that TO group was Captain Mladenovic. I was in that area as an operative from the superior command, the command superior to this brigade, co-ordinating the work of several units of the JNA and the Territorial Defence in this territory where this 4th Brigade was. And you can understand this also if you see that here there is no establishment rank that would be appropriate for that particular duty. This is an operative assignment. It's not an assignment to a duty by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it says that in December 1991 you were sent to the TO in the Krajina, to the TO staff 3 OZ - I don't know what that means - in Glina. The name of the unit was Banija-Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the Yugoslav People's Army at the time was being restructured, the units that were in that area, and that was followed by the arrival of UNPROFOR, the area that was under the responsibility of the command of the 1st Operations Group for Kordun and Banija actually formed two operations zones. That's what it means, OZ, operations zone. One was in charge of Kordun and the other one was in charge of Banija. I was assigned to the 3rd Operations Zone; that was responsible for Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With an order by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, in April 1992 you were sent to the special units of the police of the MUP of the Government of the RSK to the Vojnic Garrison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following entry in your personnel file, which states the following: That on the 30th of May, 1992, you were sent by an order of the Personnel Administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia to the 1st Army. The garrison was not assigned. So I'm asking you whether you were ever in the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia or some other 1st Army because we need to specify?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was never in the 1st Army of the Army of Yugoslavia. This order was written at the time when the Yugoslav People's Army was withdrawing from the Serbian Krajina territory. In order to maintain the status of members of the Yugoslav People's Army in some way, it was formally decided that officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, according to their wishes, could state where they would be formally assigned within the Yugoslav People's Army. And this is where this entry comes from. One of the main intentions here was aimed at resolving some questions of their status of senior officers who were withdrawing with the units and the commands of the Yugoslav People's Army to the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you withdrew or you remained in the territory of the Serbian Krajina and what happened after that in terms of your career. We don't actually see that here.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any dilemmas there. I remained in that area because I thought that if the people in that area were in danger, I as an officer for whose education the taxes of those people paid, I should stay there and defend them together with the people whose only given task by the state was to pay taxes and to send their sons to the army. It would have been immoral if I hadn't stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to talk about that later, but the Serbian Army of the Krajina was formed later. Did you have any duties within that army; and if so, which ones and when? If you can please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This question, Mr. Lukic, arises from the fact that I gave a slightly broader answer to your previous question, and I didn't actually answer the question that you put to me. You asked me about these special units of the milicija, and I didn't respond to that question. The special police units existed before the formation of the Serbian Army of the Krajina; and as you can see, from here I was sent to those special police units pursuant to a formal order, and I was assigned as the commander of the 80th Brigade of the special police units which remained in the area. After that comes what you asked me. In late 1992, I became a commander or the commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long were you commander of the Army of the Serb Republic of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: From the end of October 1992 until February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that -- just a moment, please. Maybe I have to correct you; you said February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: 1994. Mistake. Mistake. And I see that that's the way it was written here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go through the document later. After February 1994, where were you, which duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The particular post was called the Deputy Commander-in-Chief for National Security and International Relations, and more often it was defined as Assistant Supreme Commander for National Security and International Relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Supreme commander of which army, and which state does this pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb Army of the Krajina in the Serb Republic of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic, at page 10, line 18, the question is: "How long were you commander of the Army of the Serb Republic of the Krajina?" And we are given the period as October 1992 to February 1994. Now, at page 25, line 3, the witness now says: "The particular post was called the Deputy Commander-in-Chief for National Security and International Relations ..." Now, was he a commander of the SVK or was he a deputy Commander-in-Chief for national security and international relations, and what is the difference between these two?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It was probably with the question that I put afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I perhaps confused you. Perhaps it wouldn't be right -- actually, after you were no longer commander of the Serb Republic of the Krajina, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he have any other duties after that, that is to say, after February 1994, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I then understand that after February 1994 he came down from being commander of the SVK to a lower position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get an answer, please, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you heard the question put by His Honour Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not talk about the ranks involved in terms of these two posts in any definite terms, but I can give you my opinion. I think that His Honour is right, that in a way it was a lower-ranking position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And why was that? Why were you demoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The immediate cause, as I understood it, was the conflict with Mr. Martic concerning certain views and conclusions in terms of assessing the situation and concluding what it was that should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This conflict with Mr. Martic, who did he have it with? Was it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Martic was in conflict with me partly as well. I think that one of the immediate pretexts for this conflict was the deterioration of the internal political situation of the Serb Republic of the Krajina that preceded the elections for president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my own information, when you were then removed as commander of the SVK, who then became the commander after you of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to complete that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had actually intended to deal with these questions in greater detail a bit later because I think they are of relevance to our trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we have yet another entry there, and I would just like to put a brief question to you now and we will discuss it later. It says that on the 12th of December, 1994, you were appointed by decree of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the position of head and also assistant head of the Army of Yugoslavia for the land forces in that particular administration of the Army of Yugoslavia. General, did you ever actually perform those particular duties?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I never held that position. I never carried out those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to discuss the facts related to this entry later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in B/C/S, please, the last page. It's this page in English too -- no, it isn't. No. The last page in English, please. The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, it says here that your professional military service was terminated by a decree of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia dated the 22nd of December, 1994, and that you were relieved of professional military service as of the 30th of December, 1994. Is that when you were pensioned off, General, on that particular day, in fact? Just briefly for the time being. We are going to discuss that particular subject as well during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This order on my retirement was communicated to me on the 17th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us one more thing: Until the 17th of October, 1995, in relation to the position that you had, the deputy supreme commander of the SVK, did you hold any other position in any other army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: A duty in terms of establishment? Well, I didn't have that. I mean I did not hold an establishment position with a particular establishment rank. There wasn't an order appointing me to such a position in the army. What we mentioned a moment ago, the chief of the administration of the -- for the infantry, there were some other duties, though, that I did carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In which army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Serb Army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we clear one point up here. Part of the question at page 13, starting from line 21, was that your professional military service terminated on the 30th of December, 1994, by an order dated the 22nd of December of that same year. Now, a little later you say this order was communicated to you on the 17th of October, 1995. My question to you is: Between the 30th of December, 1994, and the 17th of October, 1995, what were you doing by way of work, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a professional point of view, I was still deputy or assistant supreme commander for national security and international relations, and in that period of time, up until the people and army left the republic of the Serb Krajina, that is to say until the 6th or 10th of December -- no, actually, the 10th of August, 1995, I performed that particular duty. From the 10th of August and then up until sometime at the end of September 1995, I was in Banja Luka, in Republika Srpska, and I did not have any position whatsoever because the Republic of the Serb Krajina no longer existed. Towards the end of September 1995, I came to Belgrade. I did not have any position then either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how was this order communicated to you on the 17th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was communicated to me personally by Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it by -- in written form or orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, he was given this task by the Supreme Defence Council, to communicate this to us orally. The orders about that were expressed in written form, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I ask the question again. Was the order communicated to you orally or in written form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this order was communicated to me orally and the order, or rather, the decree of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in written form was given to me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did it retire you with effect from the 30th of December, 1994? You're getting it in 1995, but it retires you a year earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's a question of antedating the decision on retirement. There was a legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, please don't anticipate my next questions. Just answer the question as I ask it. Were you retired on the 17th of October, 1995, with effect from the 30th of December, 1994? Did the order say that in fact your term of retirement takes effect on the 30th of December, 1994, even though you received it in October 1995? You can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to go through all of these questions later on with the witness, Your Honour, through specific documents, but I understand your interest, of course. Of course, I fully understand your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and what is being discussed must make logical sense to us, and if we don't understand, then we get to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that all in the courtroom know, but we were all on leave, there was court recess, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that you came to Serbia on the 10th of August, 1995, what was it that happened in August 1995 that made you leave the Republic of the Serb Krajina? Could you just tell us in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think he was in Banja Luka, in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, yes. Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 10th of August, I left the territory of the Republic of the Serb Krajina after a general Croatian offensive started on the 4th of August against the UN protected area, that is to say, the Republic of the Serb Krajina. On the 10th of August, as His Honour said, I came to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. We can barely hear him anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreter ask that when the witness is speaking could all the mikes be switched off because they don't hear him. So when you've put your question, please switch off your mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best. I'll make a maximum effort, although I have a bit of a problem with this machine in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at your personnel file in terms of the ranks you held, General. Let us see your promotions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us look at B/C/S page 4 in this document, and in English let us see 0611-7591, page 1. I will only deal with this last period that is relevant to our trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are your promotions as stated in your personnel file in the Army of Yugoslavia. And it says here that on the 14th of February, 1992, you got an exceptional promotion to the rank of infantry colonel; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then it says below that by a decree of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 10th of November, 1993, you were promoted to the rank of major-general of the Army of Yugoslavia. First of all, I'm going to ask you whether that is correct, what is written here?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you promoted previously or later to this same position of major-general in the Serb Republic of the Krajina; and if so, do you know perhaps when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of major-general of the Serb -- of the Army of the Serb Republic of the Krajina towards the end of October 1992. I cannot remember exactly. That is to say, more than a year before than what we see here in terms of the Army of Yugoslavia, major-general, 10th of November, 1993. That was at the time when I was appointed commander of the Army of Serb Republic of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So Mr. Lukic was incorrect to say that you were made a major-general of the Army of Yugoslavia; you were actually made a major-general of the Army of Serbian Krajina? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 27th, or sometime in October 1992, I was promoted as major-general of the Serbian Army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid confusion, this decree of the president of the FRY is the decree issued by President Lilic on the 10th of November, 1993, promoting him to the rank of major-general of the Army of Yugoslavia. This is what we call verification, if you recall. I'm actually then going back to what happened previously in the Serbian Army of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I'm -- perhaps I interpreted something erroneously, but that was the gist of what I read from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fortunately or unfortunately, this document is so unreadable that I'm not even looking at it, so I can't even look at it. There's nothing I can see there. So I'm trying to make sure that what is said between you and the witness is absolutely correct. And where there is a little discrepancy, that's why I keep interjecting, because I can't verify from this document. I see this is a Prosecution exhibit. Do you have no better copy than this, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an excellent copy. I have a hard copy here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have an excellent copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have an excellent copy. I can give Your Honour, if you like, my hard copy or a spare hard copy we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just if we could upload it into the record because when we arrive at the judgement this is what we're going to rely on and it's hardly readable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My copy, Your Honour, I will say, on my monitor is readable. I'm not sure if there's a problem with Your Honour's monitor, but mine's very legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe the problem is with my monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Registrar will try and help me. You can continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we can finish with this last entry about your promotions in your personnel file, and that is that by a decree of the president of the FRY on the 31st of December, 1994, you're exceptionally promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general. This is again by decree of the president of the FRY, Lilic, to the Army of Yugoslavia. Before that, were you promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general in the army -- the Serbian Army of the Krajina and do you know when this was?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general in the Army of the Serbian Krajina sometime in the course of 1994. I don't remember the exact date. I don't have that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have now completed my questions about your professional background. I have a few other general questions. Have you ever testified before the Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I think that Mr. Harmon will not object to a leading question on this topic. Twice the OTP interviewed you in the capacity of witness. I think this was in October 2000 and February and March of 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The first interview took place in Banja Luka when the OTP investigators were still not allowed to come to Serbia, and the second interview was also conducted at the time that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, how long have you known General Perisic? Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've known General Perisic since 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were then serving in Koprivica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you recall where he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was commander of the 73rd Motorised Brigade in the Koprivica Garrison at the time, and Mr. Perisic was in the artillery school in Zadar, training commissioned and non-commissioned officers in the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we're going to hear a lot about meetings when he became the chief of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, I think in that period, in August 1993, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the last time the witness made reference to a date was when he talked about 1989. Now you are putting your question to him and you say "... in that period, in 1993, August 1993 ..." I'm not quite sure what you're talking about. Just read from page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I just think the translation is bad and that's what's creating a problem. In the period from 1989 until August 1993 when General Perisic became the Chief of the General Staff; that was my question. Did they see each other in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what you should add in your question, 1993 when General Perisic became the commander of the General Staff. Then we know why you are asking -- you are putting the date 1993. There's nothing wrong with the translation; there's everything wrong with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I answer the question now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, sir, if you now understand it. I didn't understand it. You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand the question now. In 1989, I saw him on several occasions at an artillery training-ground where I had my artillery unit to train in the artillery training centre. My soldiers and cadets were there for training. After that, General Perisic came to the north-western front command in Zagreb to the operations and training organ, and that was when I saw him perhaps two or three times, during 1989 and early 1990 this was. From that time until August 1993, I did not see him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we're going to move to some direct questions, and that is for you to tell us briefly what I'm interested in when you were in Zagreb in the course of 1991 before you were sent to the education in Belgrade. What was the attitude or the relationship towards the JNA officers in Zagreb and in Croatia, generally, if you can just briefly tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As a consequence of the unrelenting propaganda, it was very intense propaganda which would use seven insulting terms in the same sentence, as the JNA and members of the JNA were considered as the greatest enemies, of course when the commands and the units in the barracks were thought of in the same way all of a sudden.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you know at the time? Was there any kind of secret arming outside of the structure of the state organs, and how was it, and what happened as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do think, Mr. Lukic, even though Mr. Harmon may not be objecting, that that's a very leading question. And I think you're now beginning to talk about the beginning of the war, and I think it's only fair that the witness begin to tell us what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do, would you appreciate a break of 30 minutes to rephrase your question and we come back? We'll take --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. I will use my time as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I believe the parties are now ready to make submissions on P33 and P39.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During the recess, I was apprised of the problem; I discussed the issue with Mr. Lukic; and we have a proposal. I understand that P33 and P39 both as presently in the system contain sensitive information. The proposal that I have and that -- which Mr. Lukic agrees with is that we be granted permission to upload redacted versions of P33 and P39. We will take out the sensitive information. We will keep in the other information. And it would be a public document then, as redacted. So if the Court gives us permission to upload new versions of P33 and P39, which I understood were draft transcripts and not the official transcripts, then we will upload the official transcripts with the sensitive information redacted from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand that to mean that in the system we are going to have two versions, the redacted version and unredacted version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because currently we have an unredacted version but it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My proposal would be that we put in a new -- we substitute new documents for P33 and P39. The substituted documents would be redacted, the sensitive information would be redacted out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. My problem with that is that -- and the Chamber is not apprised of the sensitive part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question really that came from Registry was: Should we keep it under seal or should we not keep it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, obviously if it contains sensitive information, we should keep it under seal for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is under seal for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the question is: Should it be under seal permanently?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's the rut. It should not be under seal permanently if it doesn't have the sensitive information in it. If we are permitted to upload a new version of P33 and P39 into the system but -- having taken out the sensitive information relating to witnesses or identification factors that relate to protected witnesses, if we can remove that and upload then a redacted version of P33 and P39, then there's no reason why that can't be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true, and I hear that that's the rut. The flip side of that rut is that then the Chamber does not know the identity. And we would like to know the identity when we do arrive at judgement; we would like to know who we are talking about. And we undertake, if you permit us to keep the documents under seal permanently, we undertake not to reveal the sensitive information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that's fine as far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understood in my conversation with Mr. Harmon is that for the needs of this trial the information which is public is needed. Mr. Harmon and I, as parties, are not interested in the confidential information contained in that document. So if the parties agree, then the things that the parties do not wish to present in the trial should not be of consequence to you either. If there was some items that were confidential but that were of interest to Mr. Harmon, then there would be some point in keeping the documents confidential. But, actually, the confidential parts of those documents are not relevant for this particular trial. So in that sense, this arrangement would then be quite appropriate. At least that's how I understood matters to stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm also -- what I've been told is what's contained in P33 and P39 is the -- on one of the pages, apparently, there's information that relates and identifies a -- protected witnesses. And what we're seeking to do is merely remove the page that has the sensitive witness identification from the respective exhibits. The 92 ter packages don't relate to those protected witnesses whatsoever. Apparently it was -- must have been a copying mistake or a copying error when they uploaded the document into court. The transcript, I am told, on one of the pages, either the beginning or the last page, there was -- or the last page, there was the next witness who must have appeared and whose identity was exposed in what is now P33 and P39. So the intent is merely to take off that last page that identifies the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if -- from the Chamber's point of view - and here let me not even say from the Chamber's point of view, let me talk for myself - I'm a bit slow on the uptake, and I find it very difficult to comprehend documents which are redacted all over the show. And I would like to get the full picture. My question is: If you take off that page, will I be able to get the full picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am told yes, you will be, because it's just one side of a page that has the sensitive information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think the Registrar will confirm that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm in your hands. You may upload the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Can we call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the parties advise the Chamber once they have uploaded that redacted version so that the Registrar might be advised accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. And then since they are currently under seal, I am requesting that the redacted versions then not be under seal but be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed they will be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, in the old SFRY, what comprised the armed forces of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were two components of the armed forces: The Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Outside of those components, would anybody be able to dispose with the weapons; and if so, in which context, weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were units of the police as well. They were armed and their reserve forces were also able to have weapons, of course only regular rifles, not any other kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were there any changes in relation to these formations after the multi-party elections in late 1980s and early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was serving in the then-Republic of Croatia. And as an officer, I had information that according to the laws at the time there was illegal arming going on, organised and implemented by the new authorities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was illegal about that arming and what were the sources of it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best if I gave some examples. At one point in time, a plane landed at the Pleso Airport in Zagreb which contained 20.000 rifles. We had information about this in the sense that the weapons were being shipped by trailer trucks from Croatia, that it was secretly obtained, and that it was being distributed on the basis of party affiliation. And it was being given to newly admitted members of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. There was also information that the weapons were arriving from Bulgaria, Argentina, and from some other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I would like you to clarify your answer, Mr. Novakovic. You told us that a plane landed in the Pleso Airport in Zagreb containing 20.000 rifles. And then you say you also had information that the weapons were being shipped by trailer trucks from Croatia. Are you suggesting that they were shipped by trailer trucks from Pleso Airport into some other part outside Croatia, or what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, if that's how I put it. As far as the aeroplane is concerned, it landed at Pleso Airport and the -- a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army seized that shipment of weapons. The trailer trucks brought the weapons across the border from the neighbouring country of Hungary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're talking about two different shipments? The one shipment came by plane, another shipment came by trucks across the border. If you could please -- yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as you said earlier, this component of the armed forces, the TO, did it also have weapons and ammunition, and what happened to that in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood, because of the deteriorating political situation a decision was made at the level of the -- of Yugoslavia, and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence that was in charge of that area issued an order that weapons of the Territorial Defence should be transferred to depots under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. The same thing was done with the weapons which were intended for the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I already referred to the period. Can you please tell us approximately the period to which this refers to, what you just described, approximately, if you can just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was -- this was in the summer of 1999 -- actually, it was the end of summer and early autumn of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. The witness corrected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You corrected yourself, sir; right? It's 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of the political leadership of Croatia in relation to these decisions for the TO weapons and ammunition to be placed in JNA depots?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: They objected to this decision. But as far as I know and as far as I was able to find out, the decision was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the leadership of the Republic of Croatia towards the functioning of the Territorial Defence at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the Croatian leadership aspired to simply turn the Territorial Defence into a republican army. However, the commander of the Territorial Defence of Croatia, General Novoselic, who was an ethnic Croat, refused that because the way he understood it this was something that was counter to the provisions of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were organised armed forces set up in Croatia; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: From that time onwards, armed forces were being created in the territory of Croatia. According to the then-constitution of Yugoslavia and Croatia and the laws that were in place, these formations were paramilitary. These oversized units were first set up within the Ministry of the Interior, and then a formation was established that was called the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you heard of Imre Agotic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agotic was a colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, a security officer who was serving in the command of the 5th Air Corps in Zagreb. He lived in the same building that I lived in, and we were - perhaps I could even say - friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay on in the JNA -- or, actually, I don't want to lead. Did he stay on in the JNA throughout? If not, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I remember that on the 23rd of July, 1991, we were in Sisak together at a celebration commemorating -- no, no, it was in 1990, the 23rd of July, 1990. We attended the commemoration of the day when the uprising against the occupier started, and that had happened in 1941. This was a date that had been commemorated throughout the existence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Later on - I cannot say exactly when - but at any rate it was in 1991, in the beginning of 1991 at the latest, Mr. Agotic joined these newly established armed forces that were under the control of the new authorities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether he held a particular position within the ZNG later, Mr. Agotic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what position he held in this National Guards Corps as it was called, the ZNG. However, I know that later on during the war he was in the military office of the president of Croatia, President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name of General Stipetic mean anything to you, and can you just tell us in a few words whether he stayed on in the JNA; and if not, where did he go?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: General Stipetic was General Perisic's boss in Zagreb for a while too. He was my boss as well during 1991, that is, while we were together in the command of the north-west field in Zagreb. It commanded most of Croatia, excluding Osijek, then part of Slovenia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point did he leave the JNA, and where did he end up?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the summer, June or July 1991, this command of ours in Zagreb, in the centre of Zagreb, was surrounded by sniper shooters and the armed forces of these newly established units that were under the control of the new Croatian authorities. General Stipetic was on leave, on vacation. At one point, while he was on vacation, these forces carried out an armed attack, a fire attack, against the command building. On the next day, General Stipetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was surprised. He saw what the effects of the attack were, and then it was publicly declared that he had joined the new Croatian armed forces, as he had put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we -- it does interest us from a historical purpose -- point of view to hear all this detail, but may I implore you to please listen to the question and try to be as brief as possible in answering the question. The question was: "At one point did he leave the JNA, and where did he end up?" Yes, he did leave the JNA. He ended up being part of this group. Then we follow you nicely. You see? Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, were you aware of any secret arming of the Serb people in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was such arming. First of all, in these Serb areas, guards were organised and patrols. They used sports weapons and hunting weapons. At one point in time, it became noticeable that some old types of weaponry appeared. To tell you the truth, I didn't know exactly where that had come from. That is what I can say about this secret arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, was there any official mobilisation; and if so, who responded to these calls?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the Yugoslav People's Army tried to mobilise some war-time units. When I say "war-time units," that means units that do not exist in peace time. When necessary, they are developed in accordance with mobilisation plans. Call-up papers were sent out, but it was mainly Serbs who responded to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these Serbs who had been mobilised were being armed by the JNA; and if so, what happened with those weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a normal procedure involved. Once these people reported to where they were supposed to report, as stated in the call-up papers, they were issued with a uniform. Most military conscripts had uniforms anyway, so they were supposed to be issued with uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, from your point of view, what was the reason for this extensive arming in the way you had described it? What kind of inter-ethnic tensions were there in the area, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please put a more specific question to me. Are you asking me about the Serb side and the Croatian side or just one of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had put a general question in -- on purpose, but I fully concur with what you said just now. There should be a distinction. What were the intentions of the Croatian side when they were arming themselves as you had described it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The intentions were to create a fully Independent State, to be separated from Yugoslavia; if necessary, even by resorting to armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On what kind of information do you base this fact that you just communicated to us?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had this kind of information as a JNA officer on the one hand, and on the other hand everyone who followed political developments in the media were aware of that too because the Croatian authorities had publicly declared this goal of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what were the reasons why the citizens of Serb ethnicity started arming themselves in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb people in Croatia -- well, perhaps I cannot be totally impartial because I belong to the same people. There was a historic memory in the minds of these people, and they remembered what happened to them when they were an Independent State of Croatia. Between 1941 and 1945 these people were exposed to genocide, drastic genocide. There was fear too, but there was also a realistic assessment as to what would follow and what would happen to them if the Croatian side is armed on the basis of party affiliation and party arming and if they remain unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there open clashes?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please ask me now in terms of the exact time-period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you. In answering the last question, you referred to a historical memory of 1941. The question is: Now, in 1990/1991, why did the Serbs arm themselves? Can you just answer that question. Why did they respond to the mobilisation by the JNA? Forget about 1941.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the one hand, there is the mass arming of Croats. In Croatian villages, gun-fire was heard from automatic weapons, that is to say that they did have automatic weapons. Serbs, only Serbs, responded to the mobilisation call-up of the JNA. Croats were not responding. So already there were two sides involved, and conditions were being created for an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for -- therefore, it was obvious that the people felt that an armed conflict would happen, the kind they still have in their historic memory from the 1941-1945 period. If I'm not being too extensive, I can give you an example. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I don't need an example. Do I understand your short answer to be the Serbs armed themselves -- the JNA mobilised and the Serb responded to this call-up in response to the secret arming by the Croats? Is that your short answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your help, Your Honour. That's the way it was. And that is what is important when we discuss this at greater length, if we do so. The Serb side believe that the JNA would, if they respond to mobilisation call-ups, would carry out its constitutional role, and that is to say the protection of the constitutional order within which they will continue to live safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether there was any incident in Plitvice; if so, did you personally participate in it in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: During the Catholic Easter of 1991, at Plitvice there was a clash between the members of the special units of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior and the local Serbs. At the time, I was serving in the command of the theatre of operations in Zagreb. I was ordered to go with General Raseta and a logistics officer and an intelligence officer to go to Plitvice to set up an operative group of the Yugoslav People's Army and to separate the two parties that were in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you actually do that? Did you act in accordance with that? You said that you were given that task. Did you act accordingly?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, General - you said that this is April 1991 - what was the attitude of the JNA vis-à-vis these conflicts? What was the position of the JNA in relation to these conflicts? I believe that the case of Plitvice was not an isolated one.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We were establishing a buffer zone between the conflicting parties, and we tried to prevent an escalation of the conflicts. Literally, physically, we were separating the two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point in time did the JNA actively take part in the conflict; if so, could you tell us what period that was and what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army at one point actively joined the conflict. The initial reasons, the reasons which led to the first instances of the JNA actively taking part in the conflict, were attempts to deblock the units of the commands and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army which were being blockaded by the Croatian paramilitary formations. At their positions in barracks, commands, depots, their electricity supply was cut off, they were prevented from getting food and water-supplies, and were exposed to fire. They were threatened with destruction. So these were the initial reasons due to which the Yugoslav People's Army joined the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into details, but can you just please tell us when these attacks on the barracks began, approximately. And perhaps you can just mention some of those cases without going into too much detail.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This began in the summer of 1991, and perhaps it would be best to give you the example of Vukovar which was presented in quite a different form, actually. The conflicts began with an attempt of the Yugoslav People's Army to deblock the barracks of the JNA in Vukovar. A friend of mine happened to be in that barracks. For 36 days, they resisted with major casualties and they were without bread for 21 days. I was also witness of such an attack in Zagreb on a unit which was going to relieve the guards of the theatre operations command, and it was attacked while it was crossing the bridge over the river.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last sentence of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could you please repeat the last sentence. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were many such attacks, and if necessary I can list them. But I think that they are well-known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, could you just repeat the last sentence of your last answer. You were telling us about the Vukovar attack, so don't go to many other examples. Just finish off this example. If you remember. If you don't remember the answer -- the last sentence, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall saying that there were many such attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you're not a historian and I'm not asking that of you, but do you know when the referendum of the Serbs in the Krajina was held and what was the referendum question and the decision? If you know when this happened or perhaps Mr. Harmon would agree that it's okay for me to give the time-frame; that way we will not be in dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I was about to object because it was a compound question. I thought we should take each question one at a time. I would rather see if the witness recalls rather than have Mr. Lukic testify, and I would ask that he ask one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is why you called the witness, to come and testify, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was sometime in late 1990. I did not take part in the referendum, so I don't really remember it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: But I think that this was at that time, and the referendum question had to do with whether you wanted to stay in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that at one point in time the Krajina milicija was formed? Do you know who formed that institution?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I would like to say that at that time I was not in that structure; I belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army then - but the Krajina police was formed by the new authorities of the Serb autonomous region of the Krajina and it existed as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the Krajina police the same thing as the Krajina milicija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, let's now deal with this period when your schooling for -- at the national defence school was suspended and you became part of the operations group command. Could you please tell us who formed it and what was the task of that operations group. We're talking about September 1991. That is what we saw in the entry from your personnel file, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The centre of military higher schools in Belgrade, I was issued an order to join this operations group. We were all assembled, and that is when I saw that the commander of the Operations Group 1 for Kordun and Banija was General Koturovic, who up until then was the chief of the Artillery Administration in the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. The Chief of Staff and his deputy in that period was Colonel Rakovic. I was assigned as the operations officer in that command. That command had about 15 to 20 officers, and I know that all ethnic groups were represented in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the assignment of the operations group?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be useful if we could see a map of the Banija and Kordun area. I don't know if you deem that necessary, but I think the answer would be better if we did have the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D164 on the screen, please. Perhaps the map will create some confusion. Perhaps we should look at P469. This is the map of Yugoslavia, the "Times" map of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you hail from the Kordun and Banija area; isn't that right? We mentioned that when we spoke about your CV.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I come from Kordun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in Kordun?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is Vrginmost in Kordun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the usher will help you and you can use the special pen to indicate where the Banija and Kordun area is on this map. Can you circle it, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can indicate -- if you can mark that area circled with blue with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you marked Kordun with a K and Banija with a B.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Some units of the level of the brigade were there, and the TO units were also mobilised. The command which was responsible for that area was the command of the 10th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army. That command was blocked in Zagreb and was not able to get to this area. It was encircled by the armed formations of Croatia and was not able to reach this area, and that's why there was a need to form a command that would be able to command the TO and the JNA units in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] perhaps we can save and admit this document so that we don't lose the information -- actually, for now we are finished with this map, so I would seek that it be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May this document please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D433. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have an intervention for the transcript, Your Honours. On page 42, line 8, the witness said, At the level of the JNA brigades were in that area and TO units. I just want to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, when you say the TO, do you know if the SAO Krajina TO was formed at the time, and were those units of the TO those units that had that title at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about September 1991 when this command was formed, the Operations Group 1 command, at the time there was still no Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina. There was the Yugoslav People's Army and there were units of the Territorial Defence which were part of the Yugoslav armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a document, please, that is Exhibit P1196. This -- the Prosecution sought to admit only some articles from this document. We're talking about the Law on Defence of the Serbian autonomous region of the Krajina, and we can see that the law was adopted on the 2nd of December, 1991. Your Honours, since this exhibit is quite big but the Prosecution sought to tender only some articles from the law, I just wanted to comment on a couple of the articles. I have prepared a draft translation in English. I would like to read it in the courtroom, though, so that I don't have to give you a draft translation. And we could perhaps use the exhibit in this way. It's only three articles that I will be dealing with; otherwise, I would have to give you a hard copy so that you can also follow the draft translation that we had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think I understand what you are saying, Mr. Lukic. We -- you're talking about two different things. You're complaining that the Prosecution sought to admit only parts of this document. Do you want to admit the entire document? Let's deal with that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And do you want to admit certain parts that were not admitted by the Prosecution? Right. Now, are those parts translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a hard copy of the translation, but this has not been uploaded into e-court yet. So I thought perhaps I can recommend for me just to simply read aloud, and then that part of the transcript could be relevant for you, so that then we don't have to translate them and upload those additional articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was: The documents that are already uploaded, the part that you want to deal with, has not been translated, there's no translation of it? Now, I think you must show the Defence your draft --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the Prosecution - your draft and then seek to tender it, and we'll have to mark it for identification until you get us an official translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think you should just read it, because then that's you testifying and not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree. I agree, Your Honours. I have prepared a hard copy draft translation, and perhaps then we can comment on these articles or we can have the witness comment on these articles. I'm going to leave this topic for later, and I can see that this was given to the interpreters. This is not that essential to me, and perhaps we can even upload it in the meantime. This is not that important right now for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, when was this Krajina TO formed, do you know? And what was its relationship to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The staffs of the TO of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, after the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was formed on the 19th of December, 1991, and then after that, in 1992, these staffs were formed. However, these were staffs that were neither here nor there. This meant that those TO staffs did not command any of the units. They didn't have any connection with any of the units or communications. They did not provide logistical support to those units. They didn't issue orders to those units, and the units did not report back to them. And this was because everything in that area, until the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army in May 1992, was subordinated to the commands of the operation groups of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "units," you are referring to TO units, aren't you? That's the distinction that you're making between the staffs and the units; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: JNA units, of course, and also, of course, units of the Territorial Defence, in response to your question that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was the point of these TO staffs when they did not have what every staff is supposed to have? Who established them and with what interest in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In my view at the time - and not only in my view - the establishment of these staffs was an element in the political rivalry between Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic. Mr. Martic at the time had under his control the milicija of the Krajina, whereas Mr. Babic - as he wished to strengthen his own position within that rivalry - then established staffs that were manned by retired officers. I am not aware of a single active-duty JNA officer on any one of these staffs. He established these staffs from the ranks of retired officers that were loyal to him in his belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a bit of water; it will clear your throat. What was the attitude of the JNA then towards the leadership of the Serb Krajina; Babic, Martic, and Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I would say, on the basis of my own experience, one of ignoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
