utterances.text: Was your -- am I right to say your question was: What was the attitude of the JNA then towards the leadership of the Serb Krajina ..." and by "Serb Krajina" you mean Babic, Martic, and Hadzic? Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you heard of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can you say to us? What was the Vance Plan? When it signed? Let's do it one thing at a time. What is the Vance Plan and when was it signed?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Vance Plan was a plan to overcome the conflicts that came into being in the area of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that signed the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: For me, that was a document of the United Nations. I am not in a position to say who all the signatories were. I know that the political representatives, as they were, such as they were, of the Republic of the Serb Krajina took part in its implementation; and I also know that in its formulation the representatives of the SFRY also took part. And, of course, representatives of Croatia as well as one of the parties involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether President Milosevic participated in the negotiations and the acceptance of the Vance Plan at all, the then-president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know as much as anyone else knows, whoever followed the media at the time, that by virtue of his political authority he took part in its creation and he contributed on the Serb side to have the plan accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the position of the leadership of the Republic of the Serb Krajina was in view of the acceptance of that plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Babic was explicitly against that plan. First of all, due to the fact that what is being referred to is the involvement of UN forces in Croatia; also because of the fact that UNPROFOR was not supposed to be at the line of conflict and to separate the conflicting parties. As far as I know, he thought that such a plan, although it said that it did not prejudge a political solution, in a way it did so. I know with certainty that pressure was brought to bear and that ultimately he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, to the best of your knowledge, what was the mandate of UNPROFOR according to the Vance Plan? First of all, what was created according to the Vance Plan? Was something new created in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, I think by the nod of your head you admit that your question is compound. Could you ask it simply. Make it a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I assume I shouldn't ask for a break now because I should complete this subject before the break, shouldn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We were just about to give you that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could you just tell us in a brief sentence, to the best of your knowledge, what was it that the Vance Plan brought?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's say that the nature of the question has been changed now. The essence was to establish a zone under the protection of the United Nations and that protection forces should be brought into that zone, UN protection forces. What I viewed as the most important thing within this mandate was to prevent armed conflicts and for the population in those areas under the protection of the UN should live without fear of any kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can now take the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the last question that you responded to had to do with the tasks of UNPROFOR in accordance with the Vance Plan. So you responded to that. Tell me, do you remember when it was that UNPROFOR was deployed in the territory of the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the early spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did UNPROFOR carry out this task as envisaged by the Vance Plan? What is your view on that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that UNPROFOR was resolved to carry out these tasks. I have no reason to doubt that. However, very soon in practice it became clear that this kind of UNPROFOR deployment, according to the ink-stain principle and without going to the line of separation itself, was not good and it did not prevent conflicts, or rather, it did not ensure the implementation of that part of that mandate which required that all the population there should not live in fear from attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to what principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, UNPROFOR was deployed in accordance with the ink-blot principle. UNPROFOR was deployed in certain limited areas within the UNPAs. Its mandate was not as it should have been in my view, in my assessment; namely, they should have been deployed along the separation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the armed formations that were in the territory of the UNPAs; what was it that the Vance Plan envisaged, and what was done in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Vance Plan envisaged that the UNPAs should be demilitarised. That means that the Territorial Defence that had stayed on as armed formations after the withdrawal of the JNA should be disarmed and they should hand-over their weapons to depots that had double keys. That is to say that one key was supposed to be kept by the UNPROFOR commands and the other key was to be kept by Territorial Defence staffs that existed. However, the units had been disbanded, and the weapons were under double key, as it were. As for armed persons, this plan envisaged that the regular police should stay on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was action taken in accordance with that plan? Is that what was actually done in relation to arms, ammunition, and the disarming of armed formations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what was done. I don't know whether you have a report here of a UN official. No, his name was Marrack Goulding. He sent a report at that point in time either to the Security Council or the Secretary-General of the UN, but he did state in that report that the Serb side had complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, in this period after the start and the implementation of the Vance Plan, that is to say from the spring of 1992 when UNPROFOR was established and deployed, did you personally have contact with UNPROFOR representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contact with UNPROFOR representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With who -- with whom did you personally have contact?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had contact with UNPROFOR officers in the then-Sector North. That happened quite frequently. And I also had contacts with General Nambiar of India, who was UNPROFOR commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of relationship you had with General Nambiar and what kind of co-operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If I were to describe our relationship, that would mean that we had ongoing contacts. I can just say what the nature of my meetings with General Nambiar was, if that is what you're interested in, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that General Nambiar was very correct, fair, in terms of understanding the UNPROFOR mandate and in his attitude towards us as well, from our point of view. I think - and I remember that very well - that at least in contacts with our side General Nambiar also viewed possible problems due to the employment of UNPROFOR units as it actually was. At the time, at the same time, General Nambiar never raised as a problem the question of whether our side was complying with the requirements of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that gentleman as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from your contacts with him, are you able to tell us what his position was regarding your implementation of your obligations from the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: All that I can say about the UNPROFOR commander, Mr. Nambiar, is something that I cannot say would apply to Mr. Kirudja. It was the assessment of all of us who contacted -- were in contact with Mr. Kirudja from the Serb side was that Mr. Kirudja was hostile towards our side. This was first of all reflected in the demands that he set, in political terms first of all. Well, I can summarise the conclusions from a conversation that he had with our side. He set off immediately and in all contacts with us what the political solution would be. He was prejudiced in a way, and it was our conclusion that Mr. Kirudja already saw us in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you ever heard of the term "Posebne Jedinice Milicije," special units of the police, and what is that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I have heard the term "Posebne Jedinice Milicije," PJM, special police units. But I cannot answer that in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask you to do that. Can you please explain what you know about that, what it is, and police give me your complete answer on this term. Perhaps I can be precise, because this term is used in documents and by interpreters. I said "Posebne Jedinice Milicije," and I used the -- and I would like to refer to the special abbreviation which is used for these units in documents and that is PJM.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the term "Posebne Jedinice Milicije," I would first like to point to the fact that these Posebne Jedinice Milicije existed in the former Yugoslavia before the war, and they were part of the Federal Ministry of the Interior, and as part of the republican ministries of the interior of all the socialist republics of former Yugoslavia. In essence and by the type of training, equipment, and the assignments they were issued, these were anti-terrorist units. These units were used for more serious forms of threats to security, and they exist in all police forces of numerous countries in the world, and these units exist in Serbia today and are also part of the Ministry of the Interior. That's what I can say about that. The Posebne Jedinice Milicije which we formed in 1992 in the Republic of Serbian Krajina were formed following our awareness that the UNPROFOR will not be on the confrontation lines and that the people - and I would like to emphasise that - if the people were to stay and live in those areas at all, we had to find a way to form some kind of shield, curtain, establish some kind of control on the lines towards Croatia which were aligned in combat lines towards the UNPAs. So we needed to have some kind of police force which would guarantee security to that population, and this is why these PJMs were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to whom were these PJMs subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The PJMs were subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina which had a special administration as an organisational unit in charge of these PJMs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the minister of the interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a document on the screen, please. This is a document from the financial file of Witness Novakovic, and it's on the Defence 65 ter list, 00182D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the 30th of September, 1992, and I would like your comment on the document, General, please. What is this document? Why was it issued?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is actually my agreement to be deployed in the PJM. It's dated of the 30th of September, and I was already carrying out those duties as of the 2nd of August of that year, and I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the bottom of the document, the last sentence: "The said request may be used only for the purpose of regulating the status in the service ..." And it's confirmed by -- I'm putting some questions to you about your service status. General, when did the JNA leave the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In mid-May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia were formed?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was either in May or April of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the JNA left the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, who did you receive your salary from until you retired?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: After I left the Republic of the Serbian Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, from the forming of the FRY and the Army of Yugoslavia, after they left the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, who paid your salary?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult, let me tell you, Mr. Lukic. So I can tell you how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime from the time that I left the national defence school in Belgrade until I returned from the breakthrough of the corridor, this is sometime -- I came back sometime in July. So up until August 1992, I did not receive a salary from anyone. And I heard later that they wanted to suspend my salary because they said they didn't know where I was. So this paper here is an official confirmation for the financial organs in Belgrade, I guess, of my whereabouts. And from that time on until the time that I retired, I received my salary from the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Novakovic, you said: "So up until August 1992, I did not receive" my "salary ..." Starting from when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 27th of September, 1991, when I left the School for National Defence to go to the command of Operations Group 1 in Kordun and Banija. The salary was not paid directly to me, and in the area where I was there was no place to go where you could collect your salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say it was not paid directly to you, what do you mean? Was it paid indirectly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The salary was on my account. It was deposited into my account. All I'm saying is that I was practically unable to take it, and I did not take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it was not correct of you to say "Up until August 1992, I did not receive a salary from anyone." You did receive a salary; you just could not access it? It was there in your account, but you just couldn't access it. So you were paid during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By whom were you paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I was not precise in the way I said it, yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By whom were you paid during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The salary was deposited to my account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By whom? That's -- my question is: By whom? Who was the authority who was paying you? Who was your boss? Who was your employer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My employer was still, as far as salary is concerned, the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And after -- after August 1992 you continued to be paid by the Army of Yugoslavia; no longer the JNA this time, but now the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Other than issuing your salary, was the Army of Yugoslavia in any other way your employer?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more question related to what we were saying earlier, and let us clarify. At the beginning we saw and you were shown a document indicating that you were pensioned off in December 1994 but the document is from October 1995. So from December 1994 until the decision was made in 1995, did you receive a salary?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I received a salary as an active-service officer of the Army of Yugoslavia until October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you were not pensioned off as at the 30th of December, 1994, unless you are saying you received both a salary and a pension for that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I didn't receive a salary and a pension. Earlier when you asked me -- I'm actually uncertain how to answer you and to be correct. As of the 17th of October, 1995, I didn't know that I was retired. There was no such document. So I was receiving my salary just like any other active-service officer. It was from that time on that I began to receive my pension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this document that you received on the 17th of October, 1995, was retiring you as at what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document that I received on the 17th of October, 1995, it states that I was retiring as of the 31st or the 30th of December, 1994, 31st of December, 1994. Thus, in December 1994; yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to your recollection, from the 17th of October, 1995, did you receive any pension covering the period 31st of December, 1994, to the 17th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was receiving my salary, but then from that time on I received my pension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a small discrepancy in the translation. This is an official translation, but you can see, Your Honours, at the top in the English translation in parenthesis after the letters "MUP" the translation service translated it as "Ministry of Defence," but I think it's indisputable that we're talking about the Ministry of the Interior of the RSK. I would just like to note this for the transcript. I think this is not in dispute. Where it says the MUP of the RSK, that is the MUP of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, other than your salary, what other rights did -- and benefits did an active-service officer of the Yugoslav People's Army enjoy?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: An officer was entitled to an allowance for working in a situation when he was separated from his family. Also, there was a hardship allowance. There were some special benefits for pilots and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about health and pension insurance; did active-duty officers of the JNA have that regulated through the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to resolving housing problems, did an active-duty JNA officer have the right to have his housing problem resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for resolving the housing problems of the active-duty personnel of the JNA, there was a bylaw based on the law of the army. On the basis of several criteria, people exercised this right; their age, years of service, the number of years you spent without having an apartment of your own, number of family members, and so on. On the basis of all of that, people were assigned a particular position on a list in terms of when they would get an apartment for their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All of these rights that we referred to now, that you had as a JNA officer, after the JNA had left the territory of Croatia, did they cease for you personally?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: When leaving -- when the JNA left the territory of Croatia and the Krajina, we were told that we who had decided to stay on in the Krajina had the right to housing, as it were, as it was put at the time, as if we were still in the Army of Yugoslavia. As a matter of fact, we were asked to say in which garrison in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia we would like to have an apartment allocated to us. If you think it is necessary, I can describe my own case which shows that things were not exactly that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us, did you act on the basis of that proposal and did you resolve your personal housing issue?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did act in accordance with that proposal, but it was only in January last year that I received an apartment, as the only general who did not have an apartment. I got the kind of apartment that I was entitled to when I became a major some 28 or 29 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please admit this document into evidence if we haven't done so already -- oh, but we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, there's no document on the screen now. You're talking about 00182D?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has not been admitted just yet. Okay. You want it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May the document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D434.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now have P1783 on our screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this document, General, and could I hear your comment then? What is this about, and what do you have to do with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from a poll that was carried out among the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time when the decision was taken for the JNA to leave that area. As you can see, towards the bottom of the document you see what the possible wishes are: to be transferred to the FRY, to be assigned to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or to be assigned to the TO of the Republic of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what was your decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is written here, that I opted for being appointed in the TO of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, that is to say, to stay on where I had been working.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, on page 61, line 10, he said the place where he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here, General, that you then stated that you had citizenship of the SFRY. I'm going to ask you whether you ever received FRY citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As for citizenship of the FRY, as far as I can remember I got that in 1997, that is to say, more than two years after I came to the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What status did you have in the period from the autumn of 1995 when you arrived in the FRY up until the moment when you were given citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had the status of refugee, like all the people who had come from there. I had a refugee ID. I was an ordinary refugee with one distinction, though. I did not receive any aid from international humanitarian organisations. I had a pension, after all. But my social status was that of a refugee without citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what military ID did you have after you left the JNA in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: After leaving the territory of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, I had the ID of an officer of the JNA as I had had before the war. I never had the ID of an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been admitted into evidence, and now I'd like us to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were appointed to the position that we saw a few moments ago and that you described in terms of the PJMs, what was your task? What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was commander of the 80th Brigade of the PJM in the area of Kordun. When I spoke of the PJM, I referred to the line, a curtain, as it were, a line of observation actually vis-à-vis the Croatian forces that were on the other side without any UNPROFOR control. But they did have combat deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many members did this brigade have?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly anymore, but I think it was about 2.000 members. As for the area, or rather, the length of that line that it observed -- that these men observed and controlled - of course not all of them at the same time on the line; some were on the line while others were resting at that point in time - it was about 140 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what was the ethnic structure of the population that lived in the territory of the zone that you covered?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you asking me about the structure of the population before the war started or at the time that we are discussing right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The time that we are discussing right now. That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the Croat population left that area, together with the MUP and ZNG forces, when they were pushed out of the area. I have to say one thing, and it's easy to check that: Namely, that the Croatian population in the territory of the municipality of Vrginmost, which unfortunately is no longer known by that name, I had some influence because I knew some people personally -- but anyway. Part of the Croat population that was in the area that was controlled by the Serb Territorial Defence, it was Serb by its character and it was also controlled by the JNA, the armed forces of Yugoslavia, these people who, from the very beginning of the conflict, were on the territory that was our control stayed on until the end of the war. And in August 1995 they met their own army there. I'm going to give you the names of these villages: Lukinici, Viseci, Bjeljevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the attitude of the population living there? What was their position in view of the fact that the JNA was leaving the territory of the Republic of the Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, it would have been better for you to be anything but a member of the JNA among these people in that area. As I had already said in response to His Honour's question in the beginning, as for the JNA and the Territorial Defence, they responded to their call-up because they thought that the JNA would protect them by protecting the constitutional order that existed until then. Now this was being considered as classical treason, something shameful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you feel then as a former JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is certain that I did not feel good. I said that to some officers of the JNA as well. Since I'm staying there, among -- as I was staying there among these people, the best thing for them would be to abolish my rank because that would only enhance my reputation among these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get clarity here. What was treasonable here? You mentioned that it was considered classical treason after you have said: "As I had already said in response to His Honour's question in the beginning, as for the JNA and the Territorial Defence, they responded to their call-up because they thought that the JNA would protect them by protecting the constitutional order that existed until then." And then you say that this was treason. The expectation to protect the constitutional order was treason? Tell us what was treason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. It seems to me that I wasn't being specific enough. These people who reported to these units, they believed that they were now being betrayed because their expectations were let down. They had expected the JNA to protect the constitutional order and thereby protect their safety. That is the essence of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the view of the people who were -- reported to the PJMs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned a moment ago in respect to another question you mentioned corridor and breaking through the corridor. Now I'm going to ask you what that was, what kind of action was this -- actually, let me not put words into your mouth. What do you mean when you say "corridor" and "breaking through the corridor"?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, after UNPROFOR came, the Croatian army started operating primarily in Bosnia. I am not going to talk about Herzegovina because General Bobetko wrote about that at length for the sake of his military glory, but that's not the question. It was the Bosnian part of Bosnia that was focused on from then on. If you look at the book about the 2nd Guards Brigade of the Croatian army, you have an exact list of the places where members of that 2nd Guards Brigade lost their lives in the territory of Bosanska Posavina. The objective of these operations, as stated by Zdravko Tomic who was then a minister in their government, the book is called "Behind Closed Doors," the objective was - to use his words - was to strangle the Krajina. He says that he thought, and that that was indeed the position of the Croatian leadership, that in that way it would be the easiest to resolve the problem of Knin and the rebel Serbs, as he had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put P469 on the screen once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could you please indicate to us what the corridor was and what breaking through the corridor meant. So could you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that for me as a soldier this map is quite small for me to be able to point this out precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not asking you to do that. This is not an exact professional debate. It's only for the purposes of us being able to orient ourselves. Anyway, General, please continue. Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: These units of the Croatian army, regular Croatian army, including units of the Croatian Defence Council from Bosnia and Herzegovina and units under the control of Alija Izetbegovic, cut the road leading from the Serbian Krajina and the Bosnian part of the Krajina towards Serbia. In this area, there were now existential problems beginning to crop up. There was no electricity. There was nothing to be bought in the shops in terms of food. If you had something growing in the fields, that was it. There were no medicines. There was no fuel, oil. There was nothing that was essential for normal day-to-day life. I think that the sick were particularly in danger, especially the chronically sick, as well as children. And in this situation the decision was made to resolve the question of survival by breaking through the corridor towards Belgrade as the only available area or zone at the time where all of these problems could be resolved. There was no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in this operation of breaking through the corridor, and who engaged you in this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did take part in the breakthrough of the corridor as a commander of a tactical group. I was not sent to the corridor by anyone. I went there as a volunteer. I was appointed as commander of the tactical group by Mr. Martic and General Talic after the first failed -- the first failed attempt to breakthrough the corridor. That was when it was decided that I should head up this tactical group which was on that axis and to try to break through this corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what duties General Talic was performing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The actions were underway in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps, whose commander he was, and this was in his -- in the area of responsibility of his first subordinated group, that was the 1st Operations Group Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the map a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, General, are you able to mark for us where these combat operations were conducted? Well, let's wait for us to zoom in on the map a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is it. I can see sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw the line of where the corridor was that linked the ...

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and you can put the number 1 on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the corridor linked up which territories?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that it linked up the territory of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, then this area here. Let's say that we can mark that with a 3. And it also linked the territory of the Bosnian Krajina from Banja Luka via Sanski Most, Drvar, Petrovac, Grahovo, this area here. So when I say 3, that would cover this whole area here and also this area here which is in the Bosnian Krajina. This is on the Bosnian side of the border and the area of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina on our side, including Banja Luka here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you indicated with the number 2 here, can we just note what that is for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the Bosnian Krajina. That is also called the Krajina, but it's an area that is on the Bosnian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can you mark here with the letter B the place where this corridor was broken through by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a wider area. I am looking for the towns of Brod and Derventa from here, and now I'm trying to find Doboj. It's more or less like this. For a map of this scale, this, I think, is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now first of all, Mr. Novakovic, when you were asked to draw the corridor, you drew that line which you marked 1. Should we then understand that that line actually extends up to 3 because you want to join the Bosnian Krajina and you're also trying to join the Croatian Krajina? So that line should start from 1 and go up to 3; is that how we should understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the need to communicate, yes, you're right. It should reach all the way to 3. But I actually marked only that part of the corridor which was not under our control and where we had to fight to get through in order to create a passage. This area that was under Serbian control, I am taking it as an area where we were free to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we can finish with the map as long as we still have it in front of us. So this operation, corridor, what did it achieve in terms of this area that you marked with the letter B?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier - and this is something that General Simic who was later Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska also talked about - it was a victory in a way. If you look at books today by Croatian generals who wrote about it, they said that they could not stop their army from running away. They kept escaping, if the Court will permit me to say that. Why, Your Honours? This is what I would like to tell you. I'm not boasting or anything like that. I would like to say this because it was because of the morale of our fighters. We did not have anywhere to return to if we didn't create this corridor. It wasn't a question of whether we were going to pass or not; it was just a question of when we were going to do it and how many of us would die in the process. I am very sorry when I hear today that I was in this way creating a Greater Serbia. This was actually a question of life and death for a part of the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be assigned Exhibit D435. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another document on the screen, please. This is a document marked P1782, so P1782.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell us when the Serbian Army of the Krajina was formed; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We formed the Serbian Army of the Krajina in late October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Mr. Harmon. I would like to explain. We marked this document as a 65 ter Defence document, 00181D, but then we saw that it was already an exhibit. And this is why I called it up in this way, in order to avoid duplication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, General, for interrupting you. What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, you asked me and I answered. If you want, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the answer and I'm not going to ask you to repeat it. I want to ask you: What was the reason for forming the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: From the time the UNPROFOR came, there were a number of incursions which, speaking today, using the terminology used in the world -- in today's world, I would describe that as a terrorist incursion by armed Croatian groups and terrorist activities in the territory of a zone under the protection of the United Nations which we called the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. For example, Nuskalik is a Serbian village on the coast of the Adriatic Sea, a little bit more to the south from Zadar. There was an incursion and mostly the elderly population was killed, men and women. There was an incursion at the Miljevac plateau which is south-west of Knin and to the west of Drnis. There were massacres, killings, and bodies thrown into the fields. There were incursions in Slavonia against people who were harvesting the corn. Killings -- and as far as I know, the bodies were taken as far as Velebit, some 3- to 400 kilometres from there. This is one aspect of it. On the other hand there were occurrences when the Croatian army, in negotiations with our Serbian side, did not try to bring closer their political positions and to try to find a solution in that way. They were just bringing up suggestions in order to achieve control over that territory. They never mentioned the question of the population in those territories. All that they were concerned about was control over the territory. It was thus evident that something had to be done. In spite of the UNPROFOR being the way it was, it was necessary to begin, to start with more serious preparations for defence, if necessary, without actually going beyond the mandate set by the UNPROFOR. From the time -- and you can see this decree here, this is in late October, on the 21st of November we got an order to form the Army of the Serbian Krajina. I don't remember the date exactly. We were implementing organisational preparations, drafting papers, lists of how these units should look. But all of our weapons were still under lock and key and under the control of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see from the document the decree on appointment to post, that you were appointed by the then-president of the Republic of the Serb Krajina Goran Hadzic, the document was signed by him. Can you tell us, at the time, did you find out how come that the leadership of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina picked you? Who had a share in coming to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, unfortunately there was something which could be described as distrust, disagreement, and sometimes even conflicts among the TO staffs and the PJMs. As far as I know there were even some physical settling of accounts amongst groups or individuals. This then also carried over or spilled over into the leadership. And the way the leadership of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was thinking about my authority as a military man and the reputation that I had among the police and the TO and the army, the decision was reached that I should be the one. I didn't really consider that as an honour. I thought about it as a big job and a major obligation, and I didn't think that they could surmount these disagreements, which were so dangerous, in such a dangerous situation. There were these sensitivities, these egos, who was bigger than who. And I believe that this was a luxury that we could not afford, and I believed that I had some kind of authority among all the sides, and I believed that we could then do something properly, as I thought about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, at the time or later, did you hear of anyone from the Army of Yugoslavia or from the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was involved in the talks concerning your appointment to the position of commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing. Before I accepted this position, I talked to the then-Speaker of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, with the president of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, and with Mr. Martic, who at the time was a greater political authority. I wanted to talk to him too. He had quite a dilemma, but it was probably his assessment that there wouldn't be a better solution, so they ultimately agreed to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, after being appointed to this position, did you see Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear your answer, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Milosevic after you were no longer commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we are now going to adjourn, we will be discussing these other things tomorrow. But just tell us this: When you saw Mr. Milosevic -- actually, these encounters with President Milosevic, what form did they take?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In a group with several persons, in a group with a smaller number of persons, or in a tête-à-tête.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to suggest that we adjourn and then move on tomorrow with respect to this subject and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we are not done with you, and we'll have to come back tomorrow. But before we adjourn, I need to warn you that now that you have taken the witness-stand you may not discuss the case with anybody until you are excused from further testifying. In particular, you may not discuss it with the Defence team. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning - am I right? - yes, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
